meta.titre: Scalar and Vector Products: Angles, Components and Areas in Three Dimensions

source.epreuve_titre: GCE A/L Further Mathematics past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: A surveyor in Bamenda pegs out the three corners of a sloping plot and must give the owner the angle at one corner and the area of the plot, using nothing but the coordinates of the pegs. A player in Douala kicks a ball, but only the part of the force along the line of motion gives the ball speed. Both problems are solved with the two products of vectors. At GCE Advanced Level Further Mathematics, questions on perpendicular vectors, components of a force and areas of triangles return almost every year, and they are quick marks once the definitions and the sign rules are secure.

items: A vector in three dimensions is written $a_1\mathbf{i}+a_2\mathbf{j}+a_3\mathbf{k}$, and its magnitude is $\sqrt{a_1^2+a_2^2+a_3^2}$.
The vector from point $A$ to point $B$ is $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}$, where $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are the position vectors of $A$ and $B$.
A unit vector has magnitude $1$, and the unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf{a}$ is $\hat{\mathbf{a}}=\mathbf{a}/\lvert\mathbf{a}\rvert$.
A $3\times3$ determinant can be expanded along its first row, with signs $+,-,+$.

sections.titre: The two products of vectors and what each one measures
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Scalar (dot) product.** For $\mathbf{a}=a_1\mathbf{i}+a_2\mathbf{j}+a_3\mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{b}=b_1\mathbf{i}+b_2\mathbf{j}+b_3\mathbf{k}$,

$$
\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=a_1b_1+a_2b_2+a_3b_3=\lvert\mathbf{a}\rvert\,\lvert\mathbf{b}\rvert\cos\theta \tag{1}
$$

where $\theta$ ($0\le\theta\le\pi$) is the angle between the two vectors drawn from the same point. The result is a **number**. The product is commutative, $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{a}=\lvert\mathbf{a}\rvert^2$, and for non-zero vectors $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=0$ exactly when they are perpendicular.

**Vector (cross) product.**

$$
\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}&\mathbf{j}&\mathbf{k}\\ a_1&a_2&a_3\\ b_1&b_2&b_3\end{vmatrix}=(a_2b_3-a_3b_2)\,\mathbf{i}-(a_1b_3-a_3b_1)\,\mathbf{j}+(a_1b_2-a_2b_1)\,\mathbf{k} \tag{2}
$$

The result is a **vector** with magnitude $\lvert\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\rvert=\lvert\mathbf{a}\rvert\,\lvert\mathbf{b}\rvert\sin\theta$, perpendicular to both $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$, in the direction given by the right-hand rule. Reversing the order reverses the vector: $\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}=-(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})$. Also $\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{0}$, and for non-zero vectors $\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{0}$ exactly when they are parallel. For the base vectors, $\mathbf{i}\times\mathbf{j}=\mathbf{k}$, $\mathbf{j}\times\mathbf{k}=\mathbf{i}$, $\mathbf{k}\times\mathbf{i}=\mathbf{j}$.

| Question | Tool |
|---|---|
| Are $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ perpendicular? | $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=0$ |
| Are $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ parallel? | $\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{0}$ |
| Angle between them | $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{\lvert\mathbf{a}\rvert\,\lvert\mathbf{b}\rvert}$ |
| A vector perpendicular to both | $\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}$ |
| Area of a triangle with sides $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ from one vertex | $\tfrac12\lvert\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\rvert$ |

Always decide first whether the question wants a number (use $\cdot$) or a vector perpendicular to a plane (use $\times$).

variantes.nom: Components of a vector in a given direction
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a force or velocity must be split into a part along a given direction and a part across it, or when work done is required.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
The **scalar component** of $\mathbf{a}$ in the direction of $\mathbf{b}$ is the signed length

$$
\frac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{\lvert\mathbf{b}\rvert}=\mathbf{a}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}} \tag{3}
$$

and the **vector component** is this length times $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$, that is $\dfrac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{\lvert\mathbf{b}\rvert^{2}}\,\mathbf{b}$. The part of $\mathbf{a}$ perpendicular to $\mathbf{b}$ is $\mathbf{a}$ minus the vector component. A negative scalar component means the vector points against $\mathbf{b}$. The work done by a constant force $\mathbf{F}$ during a displacement $\mathbf{d}$ is $W=\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{d}$.

variantes.nom: Scalar triple product, volumes and coplanarity
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a volume, a perpendicular distance to a plane, or the test for four points lying in one plane is required.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
The **scalar triple product** is

$$
\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})=\begin{vmatrix}a_1&a_2&a_3\\ b_1&b_2&b_3\\ c_1&c_2&c_3\end{vmatrix} \tag{4}
$$

and it is unchanged by cyclic permutation: $\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})=\mathbf{b}\cdot(\mathbf{c}\times\mathbf{a})=\mathbf{c}\cdot(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})$. Its modulus is the volume of the parallelepiped with edges $\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c}$ and one sixth of it is the volume of the tetrahedron on the same edges. It is zero exactly when the three vectors lie in one plane. The perpendicular distance from the tip of $\mathbf{c}$ to the plane of $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ (through the origin) is the volume divided by the base area $\lvert\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\rvert$.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the turning effect of a force about a point is required.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
The moment about the origin of a force $\mathbf{F}$ acting at the point with position vector $\mathbf{r}$ is

$$
\mathbf{M}=\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{F} \tag{5}
$$

with magnitude $\lvert\mathbf{r}\rvert\,\lvert\mathbf{F}\rvert\sin\theta$, the force times its perpendicular distance from the origin. The order matters: $\mathbf{r}$ comes first. For example, a force $3\mathbf{j}$ N acting at the point $2\mathbf{i}$ m has moment $2\mathbf{i}\times3\mathbf{j}=6\mathbf{k}$ N m.

sections.enonce_markdown: A triangular plot has corners at $A(1,-1,2)$, $B(3,1,1)$ and $C(2,3,-1)$, with coordinates in metres. Find (a) the angle $BAC$ to one decimal place, (b) the exact area of triangle $ABC$, and (c) a unit vector perpendicular to the plane $ABC$.

etapes.action: Find the two edge vectors from $A$.
etapes.justification: Both the angle and the area use the two sides that meet at $A$, so write them as differences of position vectors.

etapes.action: Compute the scalar product and the two lengths.
etapes.justification: The angle needs $\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{AC}$ and both magnitudes.

etapes.action: Use formula (1) to find the angle.

etapes.justification: The cross product gives a vector perpendicular to both edges and its length is twice the area of the triangle.

etapes.action: Deduce the area and the unit normal, then check.
etapes.justification: Area $=\tfrac12\lvert\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\rvert$, and dividing the cross product by its magnitude gives a unit vector. A dot product with each edge confirms perpendicularity.

sections.conclusion_markdown: (a) $BAC\approx31.8^\circ$. (b) The area is $\dfrac{\sqrt{65}}{2}\ \mathrm{m^2}$. (c) A unit vector perpendicular to the plane is $\pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{65}}(-2\mathbf{i}+5\mathbf{j}+6\mathbf{k})$. The two methods agree: $\cos^2+\sin^2=\dfrac{169}{234}+\dfrac{65}{234}=1$.

items.pourquoi_faux: The vector product is anti-commutative: swapping the factors changes the sign. Only the cyclic order $\mathbf{i}\to\mathbf{j}\to\mathbf{k}\to\mathbf{i}$ gives a plus sign.
items.correction_markdown: $\mathbf{j}\times\mathbf{i}=-\mathbf{k}$. In general $\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}=-(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})$, so the order of a cross product must be copied exactly from the question.

items.pourquoi_faux: The scalar product multiplies matching components and then adds them. The answer is a number, not a vector.

items.erreur_markdown: Finding the vector component of $\mathbf{a}=2\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j}$ along $\mathbf{b}=3\mathbf{j}$ as $\dfrac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{\lvert\mathbf{b}\rvert}\,\mathbf{b}=4\times3\mathbf{j}=12\mathbf{j}$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The fraction $\dfrac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{\lvert\mathbf{b}\rvert}$ is already a length, so it must multiply a unit vector, not $\mathbf{b}$ itself. The result $12\mathbf{j}$ is longer than $\mathbf{a}$, which is impossible for a component.
items.correction_markdown: Divide by $\lvert\mathbf{b}\rvert^2$ once more (or multiply by $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$): $\dfrac{12}{9}\times3\mathbf{j}=4\mathbf{j}$.

items.erreur_markdown: Expanding $(2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k})\times(\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{k})$ with a plus sign on the $\mathbf{j}$ term and obtaining $12\mathbf{i}+7\mathbf{j}-3\mathbf{k}$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The $\mathbf{j}$ term of the determinant carries a minus sign. The wrong answer is not even perpendicular to the first vector: $2(12)+3(7)+1(-3)=42\neq0$.
items.correction_markdown: $\mathbf{j}$ coefficient is $-(2\cdot4-1\cdot1)=-7$, so the product is $12\mathbf{i}-7\mathbf{j}-3\mathbf{k}$. Always test a cross product by taking its dot product with both original vectors; both must be zero.

items.pourquoi_faux: Unlike multiplication of numbers, a zero scalar product also happens when two non-zero vectors are at right angles, since $\cos90^\circ=0$.
items.correction_markdown: For non-zero vectors, $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=0$ means $\mathbf{a}\perp\mathbf{b}$. For instance $\mathbf{i}\cdot\mathbf{j}=0$ although neither vector is zero.

items.enonce_markdown: Let $\mathbf{u}=2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+4\mathbf{k}$. (a) Find $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}$. (b) Find $\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}$. (c) Show that $\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}$ is perpendicular to both $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}=2(1)+3(-1)+(-1)(4)=2-3-4=$ **$-5$**.

(b) $\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}&\mathbf{j}&\mathbf{k}\\ 2&3&-1\\ 1&-1&4\end{vmatrix}=(12-1)\mathbf{i}-(8+1)\mathbf{j}+(-2-3)\mathbf{k}=$ **$11\mathbf{i}-9\mathbf{j}-5\mathbf{k}$**.

(c) $(11,-9,-5)\cdot(2,3,-1)=22-27+5=0$ and $(11,-9,-5)\cdot(1,-1,4)=11+9-20=0$. Both scalar products vanish, so the vector product is perpendicular to $\mathbf{u}$ and to $\mathbf{v}$.

items.enonce_markdown: A force $\mathbf{F}=3\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+5\mathbf{k}$ N moves a loaded trolley through the displacement $\mathbf{d}=2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k}$ m. Find (a) the work done by $\mathbf{F}$, (b) the scalar component of $\mathbf{F}$ in the direction of $\mathbf{d}$, (c) the vector component of $\mathbf{F}$ in that direction, and (d) the component of $\mathbf{F}$ perpendicular to $\mathbf{d}$.
items.solution_markdown:
First $\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{d}=3(2)+(-1)(1)+5(2)=15$ and $\lvert\mathbf{d}\rvert=\sqrt{4+1+4}=3$.

(a) $W=\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{d}=$ **$15\ \mathrm{J}$**.

(b) Scalar component $=\dfrac{15}{3}=$ **$5\ \mathrm{N}$**.

(c) Vector component $=\dfrac{15}{9}(2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k})=$ **$\dfrac{10}{3}\mathbf{i}+\dfrac{5}{3}\mathbf{j}+\dfrac{10}{3}\mathbf{k}$** (its length is $\tfrac53\times3=5$, as in (b)).

(d) Perpendicular component $=\mathbf{F}-\text{(c)}=$ **$-\dfrac13\mathbf{i}-\dfrac83\mathbf{j}+\dfrac53\mathbf{k}$**. Check: its dot product with $\mathbf{d}$ is $-\tfrac23-\tfrac83+\tfrac{10}{3}=0$.

items.enonce_markdown: Relative to the origin $O$, the points $A$, $B$ and $C$ have position vectors $\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}$, $\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{j}+3\mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{c}=2\mathbf{i}+k\mathbf{k}$, where $k$ is a constant. (a) Find $\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}$ and show that $\mathbf{c}\cdot(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})=12+k$. (b) Find $k$ if $O$, $A$, $B$, $C$ lie in one plane. (c) For $k=2$, find the volume of the tetrahedron $OABC$ and the perpendicular distance from $C$ to the plane $OAB$.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}&\mathbf{j}&\mathbf{k}\\ 1&2&0\\ 0&1&3\end{vmatrix}=(6-0)\mathbf{i}-(3-0)\mathbf{j}+(1-0)\mathbf{k}=6\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}$. Then $\mathbf{c}\cdot(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})=2(6)+0(-3)+k(1)=12+k$.

(b) The four points are coplanar when the scalar triple product is zero: $12+k=0$, so **$k=-12$**.

(c) For $k=2$ the triple product is $14$, so the parallelepiped has volume $14$ and the tetrahedron has volume $\dfrac{14}{6}=$ **$\dfrac73$ cubic units**.

The base triangle $OAB$ has area $\tfrac12\lvert\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\rvert=\tfrac12\sqrt{36+9+1}=\tfrac{\sqrt{46}}{2}$. From $V=\tfrac13(\text{base})(h)$: $\dfrac73=\dfrac13\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{46}}{2}\cdot h$, so $h=\dfrac{14}{\sqrt{46}}=$ **$2.06$ units** (3 s.f.).

items_markdown: $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=a_1b_1+a_2b_2+a_3b_3=\lvert\mathbf{a}\rvert\lvert\mathbf{b}\rvert\cos\theta$ gives a **number**; it is zero for non-zero perpendicular vectors.

$\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}$ is a **vector** perpendicular to both, with magnitude $\lvert\mathbf{a}\rvert\lvert\mathbf{b}\rvert\sin\theta$; it is zero for parallel vectors, and $\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}=-\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}$.

Scalar component of $\mathbf{a}$ along $\mathbf{b}$ is $\dfrac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{\lvert\mathbf{b}\rvert}$; the vector component is $\dfrac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{\lvert\mathbf{b}\rvert^2}\mathbf{b}$. Work done is $\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{d}$.

Area of a triangle is $\tfrac12\lvert\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\rvert$; volume of a tetrahedron is $\tfrac16\lvert\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})\rvert$; four points through the origin are coplanar when the triple product is zero.
Check every cross product by taking dot products with the two original vectors: both must be zero.
